title: FDE First Principles
about: A project-based path from software architect to production-ready Forward Deployed Engineer: measure, ground, evaluate, ship and hand over AI systems for customers. A topic drops in the morning and gets one to three mornings, depending on its size: you learn it, build it and explain it on video. Each project ends with an article on rajc.work. Maths appears only when a decision needs it. About 114 hours of work: at 8 hours a week, plan on 3 to 4 months.

projects.title: Measure before you believe
projects.goal: Build one customer-support assistant three ways (rules, one model call, an agent loop), measure all three, and recommend one with evidence.
projects.math: fractions and averages, error bars, percentiles

projects.title: Grounding: meaning as numbers and enterprise context
projects.goal: Build semantic search from scratch with NumPy, measure it, plug it into versions B and C, and test it against an ontology of Acme's own terms: vectors alone, the ontology alone, or both.
projects.math: vectors, dot product, cosine similarity, matrix × vector, recall@k

projects.title: Evals that run without you
projects.goal: Turn project 1's hand-run tests into a pipeline: a judge calibrated against your own labels, paired comparisons, simulated customers, broken tools, traces, a CI gate that blocks regressions and drift alerts.
projects.math: Cohen's kappa, bootstrap intervals, McNemar's test, pass^k, population stability index

projects.title: A production-shaped full-stack agent
projects.goal: Ship version C the way a customer would run it: tools behind an MCP server, the grader as an Agent Skill, a managed cloud runtime, a React operator console with human approval for big refunds, its own identity and a Cedar policy, a red-team, and one capped run on a frontier model.
projects.math: paired differences; everything else you reuse

projects.title: Inside the model: mechanics that change decisions
projects.goal: Open the model only where it changes a customer decision: tokens and cost, temperature, long context, hallucinations, what training changes, and build vs. tune vs. retrieve. Six executive diagrams and a cost and latency calculator.
projects.math: ratios, softmax, query · key, loss and gradient descent, latency and cost formulas

projects.title: The 6-week enterprise engagement rehearsal
projects.goal: Rehearse a whole customer engagement on Acme: discovery, a security review pack, the final architecture decision, a headline-first executive readout, a handover kit, and one recorded 45-minute live simulation.

topics.title: One model call: tokens, time and randomness
topics.question: What does one model call really cost in tokens and seconds, and why does the same prompt give different answers?
topics.why: Every agent framework hides this one request. Its token counts are your cost, its seconds are your latency and its randomness is your consistency problem: the three numbers every project here measures.

topics.question: How will you know the system works, before you build it?
topics.why: Evals are the contract between you and the customer. Writing them first turns 'it feels good' into numbers. Size matters too: on 30 cases a measured 80% could really be anything from 65% to 95%; on 50 cases the range shrinks to about ± 11 points (day 7 shows why).

math.plain: A proportion is a count divided by the total. 6 billing cases out of 30 is 6 ÷ 30 = 0.2 = 20%.

topics.title: Why 30 test cases can lie: error bars
topics.question: How big must a difference be before you believe it?
topics.why: Customers will ask 'is the new version better?'. With small test sets the honest answer is often 'we can't tell yet'.

learn.title: A statistical approach to model evaluations (Anthropic)
learn.how: Read the introduction and Recommendation #1 only. Don't worry about the formulas: today's notebook builds them by simulation.

learn.title: Seeing Theory: Basic probability (Brown University)
learn.how: Play with the coin flips. How often do 10 fair flips give 7 or more heads?

math.plain: If a system is right with probability p, a test of n cases wobbles by about √(p × (1 − p) ÷ n). About 95% of the time the truth is within 2 wobbles of what you measured.

build: Simulate a system that is truly 80% right, tested on 30 cases, 10,000 times. Plot the measured accuracies.
From the simulation: how often does a 30-case test show 70% or less?
Write se(p, n). Check that it matches the spread you simulated.
Draw A and B with ± 2 × se error bars. Do they overlap?
Work out the ± range for 30, 50 and 100 cases and for your own test set. How much does each extra case buy?
How many cases would you need for ± 5%?

topics.title: Vectors, dot product and cosine: measuring 'alike'
topics.question: How can a computer hold meaning in numbers, and measure that two meanings are close?

math.plain: The dot product multiplies matching numbers and adds them up. Cosine divides it by both lengths, so only the direction counts: 1 means the same direction, 0 unrelated, -1 opposite.

math.plain: Stack all document vectors as the rows of a matrix M. Then M @ q is the dot product of q with every row, in one step. Same answer as a loop, just much faster.

learn.title: Cohen's kappa (Wikipedia)
